title: Organize the Expedition
content:
What problem does this solve?
One variable holding one value is not enough for a party roster. A list stores several related values in order under a single name. Expedition 17's registered roster is Aria, Rook, Mira, and Selene.

Basic syntax
  party = ["Aria", "Rook", "Mira", "Selene"]
  party[0]

What actually happens
Square brackets create the list. Indexing walks to a position. The first item is at index 0, not 1. party[0] is Aria; party[1] is Rook; party[2] is Mira; party[3] is Selene.

When this is useful
Use a list when you have several related values and you care about their order. Later you will learn how to add items and visit every entry. For now, creating the list and reading positions is enough.
concepts: A list holds several values in order under one name
party[0] is the first item; party[2] is the third

examples.title: Roster lookup
examples.explanation: Index 0 is Aria. Index 2 is Mira — the third name, because counting starts at zero.

common_mistakes: Using index 1 when you meant the first item (that is index 0)
Using parentheses instead of square brackets: party(0) tries to call party like a function
Assuming the example's indexes are the only ones that matter — every position has meaning

exercises.title: Predict the roster lookup
hints: The number in square brackets is a position, starting at 0.
Index 3 is the fourth name: Selene.

exercises.title: Fix the wrong member
exercises.prompt: This program is supposed to print Rook, but it uses the wrong index. Fix the index — retrieve the name from party, do not print a quoted string.
hints: Which index holds the second name?
Lists are zero-based, so the second item is at index 1.

tests.name: party
tests.message: Print an item from party using square-bracket indexing.

exercises.title: Build the roster card
exercises.prompt:
Create a list named party containing "Aria", "Rook", "Mira", and "Selene" in that order.

Then print exactly these two lines:
Leader: Aria
Scout: Mira

Both names must come from indexing into party and be formatted with f-strings — do not hardcode the names in the printed strings.
exercises.starter_code: # Create party, then print Leader and Scout lines
hints: Use square brackets and commas between the four string items.
Aria is at index 0; Mira is at index 2.
Print two f-strings that insert party[0] and party[2].

tests.message: Use f-strings so the printed lines are built from party indexes.

tests.name: party
tests.message: Read names with party[...], not quoted copies of Aria or Mira.

exercises.success_message: Roster card ready. Aria leads; Mira scouts — both retrieved by position.
